notes: Klaus governs alone (ÖVP absolute majority since 1966), so the template coalition slot 2 holds the FPÖ: in 1970 it is the only liberal party, national-liberal and the most pro-EEC force, and its populist turn only came in 1986; it keeps its MD logo. Slot 20 instead takes Olah's right-wing populist DFP (dissolved later in 1970). Slot 13 is the social-partnership Joint Commission, slot 14 Cardinal König's Church, slot 7 the KPÖ hardliners, slot 18 the expelled reform communists. Shia slots 8/9 are catchy circles of Iranian students.

0.name: Staatspolizei
0.text:
The Staatspolizei is the political police of the Interior Ministry's Directorate General for Public Security, answering since January 1968 to the ÖVP minister Franz Soronics. Vienna's position between the blocs keeps it busy: it shadows the KPÖ, the swollen Eastern bloc embassies and their agents, Arab and Palestinian activists, South Tyrol bombers and the radical student left.

Neutral on paper, its officers quietly trade information with the CIA and the West German Federal Intelligence Service and regard communism as the only real threat to the Republic. Their leverage lies in card indexes, telephone taps and the gendarmerie behind them; in a grave crisis they would be the backbone of an anti-communist emergency regime leaning on the West.

1.name: Österreichische Volkspartei
1.text:
The Austrian People's Party is the Christian democratic heir of the pre-war Christian Social Party and has governed alone since winning an absolute majority in March 1966, ending two decades of grand coalition with the Socialists. Its chairman Josef Klaus, Chancellor since 1964, leads a cabinet of experts with Vice-Chancellor Hermann Withalm and Finance Minister Stephan Koren, and faces the voters on 1 March 1970.

The party stands for the social market economy, Catholic social teaching, strict neutrality and a special arrangement with the EEC, and it has just pushed the South Tyrol package with Italy through parliament. It rests on its three leagues of farmers, businessmen and employees, the Catholic countryside and the western provinces, and it controls the chambers, the cooperatives and six of nine provincial governments.

2.name: Freiheitliche Partei Österreichs
2.text:
The Freedom Party of Austria is the voice of the national-liberal 'third camp', founded in 1956 as successor to the League of Independents. Its chairman since 1958, the Upper Austrian schoolteacher Friedrich Peter, is steering it away from its image as a haven for former National Socialists towards a liberal party fit to govern. With 5.4 percent and six seats in 1966, it hopes to become kingmaker in March 1970.

The party champions free enterprise, the rule of law against the Proporz carve-up of posts between the two big parties, anticlericalism and the German cultural identity of Austria, and it is the most fervent advocate of association with the EEC. Its base lies among civil servants, professionals, duelling fraternities and farmers in Carinthia, Upper Austria and Salzburg.

3.name: Sozialistische Partei Österreichs
3.text:
The Socialist Party of Austria, refounded in 1945 from the pre-war Social Democrats and Revolutionary Socialists, has been in opposition since 1966 for the first time in the Second Republic. Bruno Kreisky, a former foreign minister elected chairman in 1967, has rebuilt the party and mobilised some 1,400 experts to draft reform programmes for a modern Austria.

Kreisky promises economic modernisation, educational and legal reform, a shorter military service under the slogan 'Six months are enough' and an end to the stale climate of Catholic conservatism, while reaching out to liberals and practising Catholics. The party is strictly neutral, firmly anti-communist and keen on an active foreign policy. Its strongholds are Red Vienna, the industrial towns and the trade unions under Anton Benya.

4.name: Kommunistische Partei Österreichs
4.text:
The Communist Party of Austria, founded in 1918, shared power in the first post-war cabinets but has had no seat in parliament since 1959. Led since 1965 by Franz Muhri, it was torn apart by the invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968, which it first condemned, before the leadership swung back to the Soviet line and expelled the writer Ernst Fischer in 1969.

The party calls for nationalisation, workers' control, a neutrality friendly to the socialist countries and opposition to any EEC association. Its daily Volksstimme, its trading firms in the East-West business and its works councillors in Vienna and Styria give it more weight than its votes. Its real leverage lies in its close ties to the Soviet embassy and Moscow's goodwill.

5.name: Sozialistischer Österreichischer Studentenbund
5.text:
The Socialist Austrian Students' League was founded in 1968 by young radicals expelled from the Socialist student association after they disrupted the SPÖ's May Day celebrations in Vienna. Its moment of fame came in June 1968 with 'Art and Revolution', a provocative happening staged with the Viennese Actionists at the university that ended in prosecutions and sent Günter Brus fleeing to West Berlin.

Inspired by the West German SDS, it preaches anti-authoritarian socialism, solidarity with Vietnam and the Third World, democratic universities and contempt for the cosy social partnership, condemning American bombs in Indochina and Soviet tanks in Prague alike. Its circles are splintering into Trotskyist and Maoist study groups, and its leverage lies in campus agitation and the Viennese counterculture.

6.name: Österreichische Landsmannschaft
6.text:
The Austrian Landsmannschaft was founded in the 1950s as heir to the German School Association Südmark, the old defender of German speakers on the language frontiers of the Habsburg lands. Through its paper Eckartbote it cultivates the cause of the South Tyroleans, the expelled Sudeten Germans and the German character of Carinthia and Styria.

It rejects the idea of a separate Austrian nation, the Western Allies' re-education, American mass culture and the permissive society, and it denounces the South Tyrol package as a betrayal. Steeped in völkisch cultural pessimism, it wants a German-centred Central Europe standing apart from Washington's order. Its leverage lies in fraternities, gymnastics clubs and veterans' circles and in its readers among teachers and officials.

7.name: Die Panzerkommunisten
7.text:
The Tank Communists, as the expelled Ernst Fischer scornfully calls them, are the KPÖ's old guard of Moscow-trained functionaries, Volksstimme editors and managers of the party's East-West trading firms who applauded the Warsaw Pact's march into Prague in August 1968. During 1969 they won back control of the Central Committee and drove the reformers out of the party.

They demand unconditional loyalty to the CPSU and see Austria's neutrality as a shield for friendship with the socialist camp. Their ideal is a people's democracy on the Soviet model, guarded by a disciplined party and reliable security organs. Their leverage lies in Soviet and East German money, in lucrative trading monopolies and in the goodwill of the Soviet embassy in Vienna.

8.name: Ershad-Kreis
8.text:
The Ershad Circle gathers devout Iranian students at the universities of Vienna and Graz who copy and discuss the lectures Ali Shariati gives at the Hosseiniyeh Ershad in Tehran and admire Mehdi Bazargan's Freedom Movement of Iran, whose leaders have spent years in the Shah's prisons. They meet in student hostels and keep their distance from the Marxist-led Iranian student confederation.

They dream of an Iran freed from the Shah's autocracy and from American tutelage, governed by a constitution, social justice and an Islam renewed by reason and science, rejecting both rule by the clergy and godless communism. Their influence in Austria is negligible, but they are a future elite who will carry these ideas home.

9.name: Die Najaf-Getreuen
9.text:
The Najaf Loyalists are a handful of pious Iranian students and sons of bazaar merchants in Vienna who follow Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, exiled by the Shah in 1964 and now teaching in the Iraqi shrine city of Najaf. They pass on his sermons and letters through couriers and pilgrims and send religious dues to his representatives.

They demand the overthrow of the Shah, whom they call a servant of America and Israel, and a state guided by the Shia jurists, with the sharia replacing his secular laws. They reject the White Revolution as an assault on Islam and despise communism as much as the West. Their leverage in Austria is nil, but their network reaches back into the seminaries of Qom and the mosques of Tehran.

10.name: Moslemischer Sozialdienst
10.text:
The Muslim Social Service was founded in Vienna in the early 1960s to serve the country's Muslims, a community of some twenty thousand Bosnian émigrés, Turkish and Yugoslav guest workers, Arab students and diplomats. It organises Friday prayers in rented rooms, burials, welfare and religious instruction for children.

Loyal to the Republic and wary of politics, it seeks the formal recognition of an Islamic religious community under the Islam Act of 1912, a legacy of the Habsburg annexation of Bosnia. It cultivates the Muslim embassies and the Muslim World League, hoping for Saudi money to build a proper mosque in Vienna. Its leverage lies in its legal standing and its diplomatic patrons rather than in numbers.

11.name: Hizb ut-Tahrir
11.text:
Hizb ut-Tahrir was founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by the Islamic judge Taqiuddin al-Nabhani, who now directs it from hiding in Beirut. Banned and hunted in Jordan, Syria and Iraq after repeated attempts to win over army officers for a coup, it spreads its ideas among Jordanian and Palestinian students at the universities of Vienna and Graz.

The party rejects nationalism, democracy and every existing Muslim government, demanding a single caliphate that would unite the Islamic world under the sharia and confront both American and Soviet power. It works through disciplined study circles and leaflets rather than open violence. In Austria its leverage is minimal, but its cadres train a generation that will carry the call home.

12.name: Jama'at al-Ikhwan al-Muslimin
12.text:
The Muslim Brotherhood, founded in Egypt in 1928 by Hasan al-Banna, has been crushed by Nasser: Sayyid Qutb was hanged in 1966 and the Supreme Guide Hasan al-Hudaybi sits in prison. Exiled Egyptian and Syrian Brothers, linked to Said Ramadan's Islamic Centre in Geneva, organise prayer rooms and Islamic student societies among Arab students in Vienna and Graz.

The Brotherhood preaches the gradual Islamisation of society and state under the Koran and the sharia, rejects Arab socialism and atheist communism and condemns Western support for Israel, even as it finds shelter in the West. Its strength lies in educated cadres, Saudi patronage and students who will return home as engineers, doctors and teachers.

13.name: Paritätische Kommission für Lohn- und Preisfragen
13.english: Joint Commission on Wages and Prices
13.native_full: Paritätische Kommission für Lohn- und Preisfragen
13.text:
The Joint Commission on Wages and Prices was created in 1957 by Chancellor Julius Raab and union leader Johann Böhm as a temporary body to curb inflation and has become the heart of Austria's social partnership. Chaired by the Chancellor, it brings together the Federal Chamber of Commerce, the Chambers of Labour and Agriculture and the Trade Union Federation under Anton Benya, and it decides unanimously behind closed doors.

Critics call it the shadow government: wages, prices and much economic legislation are settled here before parliament ever sees them. It stands for social peace, consensus above party strife and a neutral Austria spared the strikes of its neighbours. Should the parties fail, its men could run the country as a technocratic directorate.

14.name: Katholische Kirche in Österreich
14.text:
The Catholic Church, to which nearly nine in ten Austrians belong, is led by Cardinal Franz König, Archbishop of Vienna since 1956 and chairman of the Bishops' Conference. Since the Mariazell Manifesto of 1952 proclaimed a free Church in a free society, it has withdrawn from party politics, loosened its ties to the ÖVP and sought peace with the Socialists.

König heads the Vatican's Secretariat for Non-Believers, and his foundation Pro Oriente builds bridges to the churches behind the Iron Curtain, giving Vienna a role between the blocs. The Church defends Catholic schools, the family and the abortion ban against socialist plans for penal reform. Its leverage lies in its pulpits, Catholic Action, the Concordat and the loyalty of the countryside.

15.name: Vereinigung Österreichischer Industrieller
15.text:
The Federation of Austrian Industries is the voluntary association of the country's private industrial companies, organised anew after 1945. Unlike the chambers it is free of compulsory membership and party control, which makes it the most outspoken voice of the owners of textile, paper, chemical, building and engineering firms and of their private bankers.

It fights the expansion of the vast nationalised sector, gathered since 1967 in a state holding company, and campaigns for lower taxes, investment incentives and the fastest possible association with the EEC. It quietly finances the ÖVP and, when useful, the FPÖ. Its leverage lies in money, in its ties to the Federal Chamber of Commerce and in the export industry on which the schilling depends.

16.name: Österreichischer Wirtschaftsbund
16.text:
The Austrian Business League is one of the three leagues that make up the ÖVP, speaking for shopkeepers, craftsmen, innkeepers, hauliers and the owners of small and medium-sized firms. Its dominant figure is Rudolf Sallinger, president of the Federal Chamber of Commerce since 1964, and through the chamber elections it controls the whole of commercial self-government.

It wants lower taxes, less red tape, an end to the creeping expansion of the nationalised industries and protection of the self-employed against union demands. Its liberal intellectuals look to the Austrian School of economics, whose leading living figure, Friedrich August von Hayek, returned home in 1969 to teach in Salzburg. Its leverage lies in the chambers and in the party's purse.

17.name: Österreichischer Naturschutzbund
17.text:
The Austrian Nature Conservation League is the country's oldest conservation society, active since before the First World War and organised in provincial branches of teachers, foresters, mountaineers and naturalists. Its finest hour was the campaign that saved the Krimml Waterfalls from a hydroelectric scheme, and 1970, proclaimed European Conservation Year by the Council of Europe, gives it a new platform.

It calls for a national park in the Hohe Tauern, protection of alpine valleys and Danube wetlands from dams and motorways, and action against the fouling of rivers and lakes by industry and sewage. Politically neutral and mostly conservative in temper, it has little organised power, but it voices a growing unease about the price of the economic miracle.

18.name: Die Reformkommunisten
18.text:
The Reform Communists are the intellectuals and trade unionists who broke with the KPÖ leadership over the crushing of the Prague Spring. Their figurehead is the writer Ernst Fischer, education secretary in the provisional government of 1945, expelled in 1969 for denouncing Soviet 'tank communism'; beside him stands the party's leading theoretician Franz Marek, whose expulsion is only a matter of time.

They call for a democratic, pluralist socialism independent of Moscow and Washington alike, dialogue with Catholics and social democrats, and workers' self-management. Many of the party's intellectuals have followed them out. Their leverage lies in their intellectual prestige, their contacts with Italian communists and Yugoslav reformers, and the journals they write for across the European left.

19.name: Marxistisch-Leninistische Partei Österreichs
19.text:
The Marxist-Leninist Party of Austria was founded in the mid-1960s by former KPÖ members who sided with Mao Zedong in the Sino-Soviet split, making it one of the early Maoist parties of Western Europe. It publishes its own paper, looks to Beijing and Enver Hoxha's Albania for recognition and draws new recruits from students radicalised in 1968.

It denounces the Soviet Union as revisionist and social-imperialist and the KPÖ as its lackey, while condemning American imperialism in Vietnam. Its programme is a proletarian revolution guided by Mao Zedong Thought and a dictatorship of the proletariat. Small and sectarian, it relies on Chinese goodwill, a few factory cells and the energy of the new student radicals.

20.name: Demokratische Fortschrittliche Partei
20.text:
The Democratic Progressive Party was founded in 1965 by Franz Olah, former head of the Trade Union Federation and Interior Minister, after the SPÖ expelled him in a bitter power struggle. Olah's tirades against party bosses, the Proporz system and the Red establishment won it almost 150,000 votes in 1966, though no seat in parliament.

The party courts the little man with a mixture of anti-communism, hostility to bureaucracy and demagogic appeals to resentment, including thinly veiled antisemitic barbs. Its fortunes collapsed when Olah was convicted in 1969 for misusing union funds, and it faces near-extinction in the March 1970 election. Its remaining leverage lies in Olah's charisma, his old union networks and the sympathy of the tabloid press.

21.name: Nationaldemokratische Partei
21.text:
The National Democratic Party was founded in 1967 by Norbert Burger, a veteran of the German-national student fraternities who found the FPÖ far too moderate. Burger is notorious for his role in the South Tyrol bombing campaign of the 1960s, for which an Italian court sentenced him in absentia, and his tiny party gathers the hard core of the pan-German far right.

It denies the existence of an Austrian nation, demands the union of all Germans, glorifies the Wehrmacht generation, rejects the 'lies' of re-education and agitates against foreign workers and Marxism in every form. Neo-Nazi in all but name, it lives on the edge of the Prohibition Act banning National Socialism. Its leverage lies in militant youth and fraternity networks.

22.name: Bundesheer
22.text:
The Austrian Armed Forces were rebuilt after the State Treaty of 1955 as a conscript army pledged to defend the country's permanent neutrality. They answer to Defence Minister Georg Prader of the ÖVP and the General Troop Inspector Erwin Fussenegger, and their hesitant deployment during the Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia in August 1968 exposed how thin their strength really is.

The officer corps, whose senior ranks served in the Wehrmacht, is conservative, anti-communist and resentful of politicians who starve defence, above all of the Socialist promise to cut national service to six months. It sees itself as the guardian of the Republic's sovereignty between the blocs. Should civil order collapse, it is the only force able to impose a national emergency regime.

23.name: Haus Habsburg-Lothringen
23.text:
The House of Habsburg-Lorraine ruled Austria until 1918 and was banished by the Habsburg Law of 1919. Its head, Otto von Habsburg, son of the last Emperor Karl, renounced his claims to the throne in 1961; after years of bitter controversy he was finally allowed to enter Austria in 1966. He lives in Pöcking in Bavaria and is vice-president of the Paneuropean Union.

Small legitimist circles still hope for a restoration, but Otto himself champions a Christian, federal and united Europe against Soviet communism. The dynasty symbolises the old supranational Central Europe from Bohemia to the Adriatic. Its leverage lies in nostalgia among older Catholics, aristocrats and veterans of the imperial army, and in Otto's wide European connections.
